quote: It is no longer possible for the voters to condition on the facts alone; they must condition on the additional fact of their presentation, and infer the existence of hidden evidence.
content: The unraveling result supports the essay. It proves that a skeptical receiver who knows the questionnaire exists will "infer the existence of hidden evidence," which is the essay's own sentence, and that in equilibrium the sender therefore discloses everything, which is the essay's standard (Milgrom 1981). The theorem describes an idealized receiver. Tested on real audiences, the skepticism is too weak: receivers read non-disclosure as bad news, but not bad enough, so senders profit from staying quiet (Jin, Luca & Martin 2021). That gap is the exploit the campaign manager is tempted to use. The fact that no campaign meets the standard is the essay's premise, and it opens by saying so: "Sorry. It can't be done."

quote: Whatever actually decides your bottom line, is the only thing you can honestly write on the lines above.
content: Nisbett & Wilson studied spoken reports about intuitive judgments already made, and the essay's procedure is built to route around exactly that. Writing a checklist first and then processing it moves the decision out of the unobservable process and onto paper. When a written rule does the deciding, the printed reasons cause the conclusion by construction, and that is the whole case for improper linear models over clinical judgment (Dawes 1979). How the weights were chosen is a fair question. It is also a question anyone can ask of a published checklist and nobody can ask of an unpublished intuition. The essay tells the manager to hand voters the algorithm, which is the most honest disclosure possible when introspection is unreliable.
